module: Haematological Emergencies in ICU Part II

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: A 24-year-old man with HbSS disease is on day 3 of an admission for a painful crisis. He develops pleuritic chest pain, a respiratory rate of 30/min and SpO2 88% on air, and a chest radiograph shows new right lower lobe consolidation. Which statement best describes his diagnosis?
options: This is community-acquired pneumonia, since acute chest syndrome requires a negative chest radiograph
The diagnosis cannot be made during an established painful crisis, as acute chest syndrome only occurs de novo
Acute chest syndrome cannot be diagnosed without fever, a mandatory component of the definition
Acute chest syndrome requires demonstration of pulmonary embolism on CT before the diagnosis can be made
He meets the definition of acute chest syndrome: a new infiltrate plus two of pleuritic pain, hypoxaemia, tachypnoea or fever
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome is defined as a new infiltrate on chest imaging together with any two of pleuritic chest pain, hypoxaemia, tachypnoea or fever — this patient has three of the four. No single feature is mandatory, and fever is only common rather than universal in adults. It typically develops within the first three to four days of an acute pain episode, so occurring during an established crisis is the expected pattern rather than an argument against it. The clinical overlap with pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, fluid overload and opioid-induced hypoventilation is precisely why vigilance is required.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: A 31-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has acute chest syndrome. Over 12 hours her oxygen requirement rises from 2 to 10 L/min despite antibiotics and analgesia. Her haemoglobin is 96 g/L, which is at her usual baseline. What is the most appropriate transfusion strategy?
options: Exchange transfusion, indicated for severe disease or deterioration without anaemia
Give an exchange transfusion only once invasive mechanical ventilation has been started
Withhold transfusion entirely, since her haemoglobin is at baseline
Transfuse only if the haemoglobin falls more than 2 g/dL below baseline
Simple top-up transfusion of two units, which achieves an equivalent reduction in circulating sickle cells
questions.explanation: Exchange transfusion is indicated for severe disease or for patients who deteriorate without being anaemic, because its benefit lies in reducing the proportion of circulating sickle cells rather than simply adding oxygen-carrying capacity. A simple top-up improves oxygenation but does not reduce HbS%, which is the therapeutic target here, and waiting for a fall in haemoglobin or for intubation would forfeit the window in which transfusion produces rapid clinical and radiological improvement. Exchange typically aims for an HbS below 30 to 40% depending on the situation.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease is admitted with acute chest syndrome. Blood and sputum cultures are sent and are as yet negative. Which antimicrobial approach is most appropriate?
options: Narrow-spectrum cover against Streptococcus pneumoniae alone, as this is the dominant pathogen
Empirical antibiotics including atypical cover, started immediately
Empirical antifungal therapy, since invasive fungal infection is the commonest trigger
Withhold antibiotics until a pathogen is identified, to limit unnecessary antimicrobial exposure
Antiviral therapy alone, as bacterial infection does not precipitate acute chest syndrome
questions.explanation: Because the causes of acute chest syndrome — in situ sickling, fat embolism, thromboembolism and infection — cannot be reliably distinguished at the bedside, infection is assumed and empirical antibiotics are given even without positive microbiology. Atypical cover matters because Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae and viral infections are the commonest infective triggers, so narrow pneumococcal cover would miss the likeliest organisms. Waiting for cultures in a condition that can progress from mild hypoxia to respiratory failure within hours is not defensible.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: A 27-year-old man with acute chest syndrome is being monitored on the ward. Which of the following findings is a recognised indicator of severity that should prompt escalation?
options: A fall in platelet count of more than 20% from baseline
Unilobar rather than multilobar consolidation on chest radiograph
A rise in platelet count of more than 20% from baseline
A reticulocyte count above the patient's baseline
A haemoglobin that remains stable at the patient's usual baseline
questions.explanation: Severity indicators include progressive respiratory failure, a fall in platelet count exceeding 20% of baseline and a fall in haemoglobin of more than 2 g/dL from baseline; multilobar involvement, neurological symptoms and pre-existing cardiac disease at presentation also predict complications. A rising platelet count and a stable haemoglobin are reassuring rather than concerning, and unilobar disease carries a better outlook than multilobar. A rising reticulocyte count reflects marrow response rather than deterioration.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Sickle Cell Disease
questions.question: All of the following are recognised precipitants of a sickle cell crisis EXCEPT:
options: Hypoxia
Dehydration
High altitude
Infection
Hypercalcaemia
questions.explanation: Recognised precipitants are stress, pain, dehydration, temperature change, high altitude, infection and hypoxia — a list that explains why management centres on rehydration, correcting hypoxia, treating infection, adequate analgesia and keeping the patient warm. Hypercalcaemia has no established role as a trigger. The common thread among the genuine precipitants is that each either promotes deoxygenation of haemoglobin S or increases blood viscosity, both of which favour polymerisation and sickling.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: A 22-year-old woman with a thoracic vaso-occlusive crisis is in severe pain and is splinting her chest. Which statement best describes the role of analgesia?
options: Fixed high-dose opioid infusion without titration gives the best protection against atelectasis
Opioids should be avoided altogether because of the risk of respiratory depression in sickle cell disease
Analgesia should be withheld until acute chest syndrome has been excluded radiologically, to avoid masking deterioration
Prompt analgesia, carefully titrated to avoid opioid-induced hypoventilation
Analgesic requirements are unrelated to ventilation and can be managed independently of respiratory monitoring
questions.explanation: Untreated thoracic pain causes chest splinting and hypoventilation, leading to atelectasis and worsening sickling, so adequate analgesia is protective rather than optional. The countervailing risk is that excessive opioid causes hypoventilation and hypoxia, itself a driver of further sickling — which is why the requirement is careful titration to effect rather than either withholding or fixed high dosing. Adequate analgesia is also what makes incentive spirometry feasible, adding a second route to reducing atelectasis.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Sickle Cell Disease
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease is established on hydroxyurea as long-term therapy. By what mechanism does it act?
options: Stimulation of erythropoietin release from the peritubular cells of the kidney
Reversible inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase, raising foetal haemoglobin
Irreversible inhibition of the beta-globin gene promoter, preventing HbS synthesis
Inhibition of terminal complement at the C5 protein
Direct chelation of free haem released into plasma during intravascular haemolysis
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea reversibly inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, suppressing erythroid progenitors and raising foetal haemoglobin levels; because HbF interferes with HbS polymerisation, this reduces crisis frequency, reduces transfusion requirement and improves overall survival. Haem scavenging by agents such as haemopexin remains a future therapy rather than an established one, and C5 inhibition belongs to complement-mediated disease including hyperhaemolysis syndrome. Erythropoietin is used to stimulate erythropoiesis in hyperhaemolysis, not as disease-modifying therapy in sickle cell disease.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: A patient with acute chest syndrome deteriorates and requires invasive mechanical ventilation. Which ventilatory strategy is recommended?
options: Permissive hypoxaemia with an SpO2 target of 85 to 88%, limiting oxygen toxicity and ventilator-induced injury
Tidal volumes of 6 ml/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O
Zero end-expiratory pressure to avoid impeding pulmonary blood flow
High tidal volumes with plateau pressures up to 40 cmH2O to overcome reduced compliance
Tidal volumes of 10 ml/kg predicted body weight to maximise alveolar recruitment
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome can progress to ARDS, and the same lung protective principles apply: 6 ml/kg predicted body weight with plateau pressures kept below 30 cmH2O. Positive airway pressure — whether by high-flow nasal oxygen, CPAP, non-invasive or invasive ventilation — helps by increasing functional residual capacity and compliance, so zero PEEP would remove the main physiological benefit. Permissive hypoxaemia is particularly dangerous here, since a falling alveolar oxygen tension directly drives further sickling; the recommended target is an SpO2 above 94%. ECMO may have a role in refractory cases although the evidence base is thin.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease is admitted with suspected acute chest syndrome. Which investigation should be prioritised specifically because of a problem characteristic of this patient group?
options: Early D-dimer, because a normal result excludes acute chest syndrome
Early bronchoscopy, because it is required to confirm the diagnosis
Early crossmatch, because alloimmunisation delays finding compatible blood
Early echocardiography, because acute valvular failure is the usual cause of deterioration
Early bone marrow aspirate, because marrow infarction must be confirmed histologically
questions.explanation: Red cell alloimmunisation is common in repeatedly transfused sickle cell patients, so finding compatible blood can take considerable time — sending the crossmatch early avoids a delay at the moment transfusion becomes urgent. The standard workup otherwise comprises chest radiograph, full blood count, biochemistry, arterial blood gas when SpO2 is below 94%, and microbiological sampling including atypical and viral screens. D-dimer cannot exclude the syndrome, and neither bronchoscopy nor marrow sampling is part of routine diagnosis.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Sickle Cell Disease
questions.question: Regarding sickle cell disease and its complications, decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Fat embolism from vaso-occlusive bone marrow infarction can precipitate acute chest syndrome and multi-organ failure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Silent cerebral infarcts are rare in sickle cell disease.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Splenic infarction leading to functional asplenia is why antibiotic prophylaxis is routinely used.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Average life expectancy in sickle cell disease is now comparable to that of the general population.

questions.explanation: Bone marrow infarction releases fat globules systemically and is one of the recognised mechanisms of acute chest syndrome, alongside in situ sickling, thromboembolism and infection. Silent cerebrovascular infarcts are common rather than rare and carry an increased risk of cognitive impairment, which is one reason acute ischaemic stroke is an indication for exchange transfusion. Repeated splenic infarction produces functional asplenia and a high risk of infection with encapsulated organisms, hence routine antibiotic prophylaxis. Despite improvements in care, average life expectancy remains around twenty years shorter than in the general population.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: Regarding the pathophysiology and clinical features of acute chest syndrome, decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Radiological changes usually appear before clinical signs become apparent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Typical bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae are the commonest infective triggers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Hypoxia is a frequent finding in adults and is a useful predictor of severity and outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It typically develops within the first three to four days of an acute painful episode.

questions.explanation: The syndrome characteristically emerges in the first three to four days of a pain crisis, when fat embolism, intrapulmonary sickling, infection or thromboembolism supervene. Clinical signs generally precede radiological findings, which is exactly what makes the diagnosis difficult and demands a high index of suspicion — relying on the chest radiograph to declare itself first will delay treatment. The commonest infective precipitants are atypical organisms such as Chlamydophila pneumoniae and Mycoplasma pneumoniae together with viruses, which is why empirical cover must include atypicals. Severe hypoxia is frequent in adults and is a useful predictor of both severity and outcome.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome
questions.question: Regarding the supportive management of acute chest syndrome, decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Incentive spirometry with adequate analgesia may help prevent deterioration by reducing atelectasis.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A target oxygen saturation above 94% is recommended.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Aggressive fluid loading to supranormal volumes is recommended to reduce blood viscosity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Antibiotics should be withheld until microbiological cultures return positive.

questions.explanation: Because hypoxia drives sickling, an SpO2 target above 94% is recommended even though the optimal level is not formally established, and arterial blood gas sampling is advised whenever saturations fall below that threshold. Avoiding dehydration matters, but the aim is adequate hydration rather than aggressive loading: fluid overload is a real hazard, particularly once ARDS develops. Infection is assumed rather than proven, so empirical antibiotics with atypical cover are given without waiting for cultures. Incentive spirometry, made possible by adequate analgesia, reduces atelectasis and may prevent progression in patients with chest pain.

questions.section: Sickle cell disease and Acute chest syndrome: Sickle Cell Disease
questions.question: Regarding disease-modifying and curative treatments for sickle cell disease, decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Successful haematopoietic stem cell transplant reverses end-organ damage already caused by the disease.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Stem cell donors for transplantation do not need to be HLA-matched.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Gene therapy requires myeloablative chemotherapy before administration, with an attendant risk of severe infection.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of crises and improves overall survival.

questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea is the established primary drug therapy, reducing crisis frequency and transfusion requirement and improving survival. Transplantation allows the recipient to produce normal haemoglobin but does nothing for damage already sustained, which is why the risk-benefit balance favours it mainly in children with severe disease before that damage accumulates. Gene therapy shares the requirement for myeloablative conditioning and the resulting window of neutropenia and severe infection risk, and offers a curative option where allogeneic transplant is unavailable. Donors must be HLA-matched, which often means relying on a close relative.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Diagnosis
questions.question: A 29-year-old woman with sickle cell disease was transfused two units nine days ago for a painful crisis. She now has jaundice, back pain and dark urine. Her haemoglobin is 58 g/L, below her pre-transfusion value of 74 g/L; the reticulocyte count is low, LDH and bilirubin are rising and HbA% has fallen sharply. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
Iron deficiency anaemia
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Acute splenic sequestration
Hyperhaemolysis syndrome
questions.explanation: The combination of recent transfusion, a haemoglobin falling below the pre-transfusion level, laboratory evidence of haemolysis, an inappropriately low reticulocyte count and a marked fall in HbA% matches the proposed consensus criteria for hyperhaemolysis syndrome, in which both donor and native red cells are destroyed. An aplastic crisis produces reticulocytopenia but without the haemolytic markers or the temporal link to transfusion, and splenic sequestration causes rapid anaemia with splenic enlargement rather than haemoglobinuria and a falling HbA%. Recognising the pattern matters because the symptoms are otherwise easily mistaken for a vaso-occlusive crisis.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Management
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease is diagnosed with hyperhaemolysis syndrome and the haemoglobin is 42 g/L. What is the single most important management step?
options: Proceed directly to urgent exchange transfusion
Perform an urgent splenectomy to halt extravascular haemolysis
Start therapeutic anticoagulation for presumed thrombotic microangiopathy
Stop further transfusion, accepting a lower haemoglobin than would normally be tolerated
Transfuse two further units of extended antigen-matched blood to restore oxygen carrying capacity
questions.explanation: Continued transfusion exacerbates the haemolysis and can prove fatal, so stopping it is the key intervention even though it means tolerating haemoglobin values far below usual thresholds, individualised to the patient's organ function and comorbidity. Further blood loss is minimised by using paediatric sample tubes and limiting phlebotomy. Antigen-negative crossmatched blood does not reliably prevent the syndrome in alloimmunised patients, so matching offers no safe route to continued transfusion; if transfusion becomes unavoidable, extended antigen typing is used alongside specialist input. Disease-directed therapy relies on IVIg, corticosteroids and, where complement activation is implicated, eculizumab.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Pathophysiology
questions.question: A haematologist asks you to distinguish hyperhaemolysis syndrome from a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction in a patient with sickle cell disease. Which feature best separates them?
options: Hyperhaemolysis destroys donor and native cells with the HbA:HbS ratio broadly preserved; a delayed reaction drops HbA disproportionately
Hyperhaemolysis occurs only within 24 hours of transfusion, whereas delayed reactions occur later
Only a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction can occur in patients without a haemoglobinopathy
Hyperhaemolysis produces a strongly positive direct antiglobulin test in the acute phase, whereas a delayed reaction leaves it negative
A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction characteristically causes reticulocytopenia, whereas hyperhaemolysis causes reticulocytosis
questions.explanation: In a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction there is an immune response against a donor red cell antigen and only the transfused cells are destroyed, so in sickle cell disease HbA falls disproportionately. Hyperhaemolysis destroys both donor and autologous cells, which is why the post-transfusion haemoglobin can fall below the pre-transfusion value while the HbA:HbS ratio remains relatively unchanged. The direct antiglobulin test runs the other way from the distractor: it is usually negative in the acute form. Reticulocytopenia belongs to hyperhaemolysis rather than to the delayed reaction, and hyperhaemolysis is described in patients without any underlying haematological disease.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Investigations
questions.question: A patient being investigated for possible hyperhaemolysis syndrome has a profound anaemia. Which reticulocyte finding would support the diagnosis?
options: A count that rises and falls in parallel with the haemoglobin
An absent count, which is required to make the diagnosis
A low or normal count, inappropriate for the anaemia
A markedly raised count, reflecting brisk compensatory marrow response
The reticulocyte count has no diagnostic role in this condition
questions.explanation: A low or decreasing reticulocyte count in a patient with worsening anaemia is one of the proposed consensus criteria, and it is striking precisely because brisk reticulocytosis is what would normally be expected. The mechanism is debated: transfusion-induced suppression of erythropoiesis has been proposed, but the response to steroids suggests peripheral consumption is the more likely explanation. Reticulocytopenia is not invariably present, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis, and a rising reticulocyte count instead heralds recovery.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Definition
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the acute form of hyperhaemolysis syndrome?
options: It occurs more than 7 days after transfusion, with new alloantibodies typically identified
It occurs less than 7 days after transfusion and is defined by a strongly positive direct antiglobulin test
Onset within 7 days, with a negative direct antiglobulin test and no new alloantibodies
It occurs only after a third or subsequent transfusion episode in a previously alloimmunised patient
It is distinguished from the delayed form by the presence of reticulocytosis
questions.explanation: The acute form presents within seven days of transfusion, and serological analysis typically shows a negative direct antiglobulin test with no new or additional red cell alloantibodies, indicating that antibody-mediated haemolysis is not the explanation. The delayed form occurs beyond seven days with a positive test and new alloantibodies commonly found. This variability in serology is exactly why the syndrome cannot simply be classified as a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction. Reticulocytopenia rather than reticulocytosis is the characteristic marrow finding in both forms.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Management
questions.question: A patient who had hyperhaemolysis syndrome three years ago now requires an elective transfusion before surgery. What preventive strategy is recommended?
options: Intravenous immunoglobulin and corticosteroids before transfusion
No prophylaxis is needed, since recurrence after a previous episode has not been described
Pre-transfusion exchange transfusion to lower the HbS percentage below 30%
Prophylactic plasmapheresis immediately before every subsequent transfusion episode
Eculizumab monotherapy commenced one week before transfusion
questions.explanation: Recurrence following subsequent transfusion is possible even many years later, although it is extremely rare, so a patient with a previous episode is given immunoglobulin and steroids before an elective transfusion; rituximab is added if hyperhaemolysis or a delayed haemolytic reaction recurs despite that. Eculizumab and plasmapheresis are treatments for established disease rather than routine prophylaxis, and plasmapheresis carries the specific hazard of worsening anaemia through the extracorporeal volume. Exchange transfusion addresses sickling, not the immune destruction of transfused and native cells.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Diagnosis
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the proposed consensus criteria for the diagnosis of hyperhaemolysis syndrome?
options: A significant fall in HbA% in sickle cell disease
Laboratory evidence of haemolysis: rising LDH and bilirubin
A haemoglobin decline to below the pre-transfusion level
A positive direct antiglobulin test in the acute phase
Recent transfusion within the past 7 days, and up to 21 days
questions.explanation: The proposed criteria comprise recent transfusion, a haemoglobin falling below the pre-transfusion value, laboratory evidence of haemolysis, a low or decreasing reticulocyte count despite worsening anaemia, and a significant fall in HbA% in patients with sickle cell disease or beta thalassaemia. The direct antiglobulin test is deliberately absent because its result varies with the form of the syndrome — usually negative in the acute presentation, positive in the delayed one — so it cannot serve as a diagnostic criterion. No universally agreed criteria exist, which is part of why the condition is under-recognised and under-reported.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Investigations
questions.question: Regarding the investigation of suspected hyperhaemolysis syndrome, decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Lactate dehydrogenase and plasma-free haemoglobin are expected to be low.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Post-transfusion haptoglobin is of limited value because most affected patients have chronic haemolysis.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Transfusion with antigen-negative crossmatched blood reliably prevents the syndrome in alloimmunised patients.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fall in HbA% supports destruction of transfused cells in patients with sickle cell disease or beta thalassaemia.

questions.explanation: Haptoglobin is already chronically consumed in these patients, so a low post-transfusion value adds nothing interpretable. Both LDH and plasma-free haemoglobin are expected to rise rather than fall, and their trend is used for monitoring. The assumption that antigen-matched blood is protective is a dangerous one: even in patients known to have alloantibodies, antigen-negative crossmatched blood may not prevent the syndrome, which is why stopping transfusion rather than refining the match is the cornerstone of treatment. Tracking HbA% is useful because a marked fall indicates destruction of the transfused cells.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Management
questions.question: Regarding the treatment of hyperhaemolysis syndrome, decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Erythropoietin and haematinic supplementation are contraindicated in this setting.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Corticosteroids can be given without concern for adverse effects in sickle cell disease.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Eculizumab acts by inhibiting terminal complement activation at the C5 protein.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Plasmapheresis may worsen the anaemia because of the extracorporeal blood volume.

questions.explanation: Eculizumab blocks complement at C5 and targets the complement-mediated route of red cell destruction, while intravenous immunoglobulin addresses the macrophage and antibody-mediated pathway. Corticosteroids, typically methylprednisolone 500 mg for two days, are standard but carry a genuine hazard in sickle cell disease because of hyperviscosity and precipitation of new vaso-occlusive crises, so the balance must be weighed rather than assumed benign. Plasmapheresis removes free haem, haemoglobin and antibodies but adds extracorporeal volume that can deepen the anaemia and is not tolerated by everyone. Stimulating erythropoiesis with erythropoietin plus vitamin B12, folate and intravenous iron where deficient is an active part of management, not a contraindication.

questions.section: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome: Epidemiology
questions.question: Regarding the epidemiology and outcome of hyperhaemolysis syndrome, decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The acute form is defined as occurring more than 7 days after transfusion.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recovery is heralded by a rising reticulocyte count followed by a gradual rise in haemoglobin.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A 26-year case-control analysis found that approximately 13% of episodes were fatal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It occurs exclusively in patients with sickle cell disease.

questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is the commonest setting because of repeated transfusion, but the syndrome is also described in thalassaemia, myelofibrosis, anaemia of chronic disease and in patients with no underlying haematological disorder at all — an underlying haemoglobinopathy is not a prerequisite. Mortality of around 13% of episodes was reported in a case-control analysis spanning 1992 to 2018, alongside considerable morbidity and prolonged hospital stay. A rising reticulocyte count is the first sign of recovery, mirroring the reticulocytopenia that characterises the acute illness. The acute form is defined by onset within seven days of transfusion; beyond that it is classified as delayed.
